source.title_on_document: Can You Make It Sound Like You? Post-Editing LLM-Generated Text for Personal Style

supplement.where: Appendices A-D, PDF pp. 13-29. The main text points to these appendices; no separately missing statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A gives recruitment, exclusions, and permutation-test details (pp. 13-14). Appendix B includes examples (Table 1, p. 15), embedding-model validation and robustness (Tables 2-3, p. 16), style-importance mixed-model coefficients/SEs/CIs (Tables 4-6, p. 18), preference rankings (Table 7, p. 19), linguistic acceptability (Figure 12, p. 20), and the acceptability/style-change mixed model (Table 8, p. 21). Appendix C contains the independent formative survey and task counts (pp. 22-24). Appendix D contains the interface and survey screenshots (pp. 24-29). The main H1/H2 effect sizes and intervals also appear in the main text. Main diversity contrasts have no reported participant-level standard errors; their resampling unit is not specified.

paper_design_summary: An online within-person experiment analyzed 81 Prolific writers who completed randomized blocks of four AI-draft post-editing tasks and two unassisted writing tasks, with task allocation also randomized (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). Automated style embeddings measured personal stylistic alignment and similarity across different writers; exploratory analyses also scored linguistic acceptability (pp. 5-7, sections 5-6; pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1). A separate formative survey analyzed 88 Prolific respondents to select writing scenarios and did not involve AI-assisted creative output (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

studies.label: Main online writing and post-editing experiment

assignment.what_was_assigned: Within each participant, the treatment and control task blocks were randomized, as described in section 4 and shown by the randomization bracket/die in Figure 1. Six self-selected writing tasks were also randomly allocated: four to AI-draft post-editing and two to unassisted writing (p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9). The PDF does not supply sequence counts or the allocation algorithm.
assignment.quote: As illustrated in Figure 1, participants completed pre- and post-surveys, task difficulty surveys, a brief tutorial, and two randomized writing task blocks (treatment and control).
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 24, Table 9 caption
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1, Introduction, footnote 2: https://aspredicted.org/ck6xk4.pdf; p. 3, section 3. The linked preregistration was not separately retrieved.

arms.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
arms.description: Participants first planned content, then edited a supplied LLM-generated draft to express their personal style. Four tasks per participant; the same analyzed people also completed the control block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). Original unedited drafts are retained as a reference stage of this condition, not a separate participant arm.

arms.name: Unassisted human writing
arms.description: Participants planned content and wrote directly from those plans without seeing any LLM-generated text for those tasks. Two tasks per participant; these are the same people as in the treatment block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 100 recruited and 81 analyzed after excluding responses from people who never edited any LLM-generated draft or did not complete the entire study. These were preregistered exclusion criteria. The count at randomization, timing of exclusions relative to assignment, and counts for each exclusion reason are not reported. The recruitment target was reduced for completion-time/payment-budget reasons, not based on results (p. 13, Appendix A.1 and footnote 13).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific users, limited to one session per person (p. 13, Appendix A.1). The same 81 analyzed writers contribute to both conditions; arm counts must not be added.
participants.quote: Following our preregistered exclusion criteria, we discarded responses where participants never edited any of the LLM-generated drafts or did not complete the entire study, leaving 81 participants.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4; p. 13, Appendix A.1; p. 24, Table 9 caption

ai_tool.how_used: GPT-o4-mini supplies a full initial draft from the participant-written content plan and the task prompt; participants then edit that draft themselves (pp. 4-5, sections 4-5.1 and Figure 2). The role is coded other: initial-draft generation followed by human post-editing. The model translates the human-supplied content plan into prose rather than supplying ideas or examples, coaching, or refining an existing human draft. The supplied AI text remains available while the treatment output is produced.

task.description: Participants choose six of eight personal writing scenarios and provide fictional planned details. Tasks include thank-you and apology letters, wedding/birthday speeches, catch-up and condolence letters, reassurance/encouragement messages, wedding vows, and eulogies/obituaries/tributes (p. 24, Table 9). Four tasks use AI-draft post-editing and two use unaided writing. Planning requires at least 30 characters; control writing at least 150 characters; the example generation prompt requests about 150 words (pp. 4-5, section 4 and Prompt 4.1).
task.duration: At least two minutes per treatment post-editing task (p. 5, section 4); mean whole-study completion time 1.69 hours (p. 13, Appendix A.1). No separate control-task time limit is stated.

outcomes.name: Between-participant stylistic diversity / homogeneity (H2a and H2b)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of LUAR-MUD style embeddings between texts from different participants; higher similarity means greater homogeneity and lower diversity (pp. 5-7, sections 5.2 and 6.2, Figure 6). H2a compares post-edited writing with unassisted writing; H2b uses the original LLM drafts as a second benchmark, not an independently assigned group. CISR is an alternative embedding-model robustness check of the same outcome (pp. 14-16, Appendix B.2, Table 3). No numerical arm means, SDs, or exact pair counts are printed. H2 is one of the paper’s two main preregistered hypotheses (p. 3, section 3).

contrasts.reported: H2a, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51]. CISR robustness: p = 0.0002, g = 1.03, 95% CI [0.91, 1.14]. Positive printed g denotes higher similarity (lower diversity) in post-edited text. Direction is coded for diversity; the printed effect has not been re-signed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2a

contrasts.reported: H2b, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = -0.69, 95% CI [-0.74, -0.63]. CISR robustness: p = 0.0002, g = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.62]. Negative printed g denotes lower similarity (higher diversity) after post-editing. Direction is coded for diversity; the printed effect has not been re-signed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3, H2b

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of style embeddings; lower similarity means more diversity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: LUAR-MUD (Rivera-Soto et al., 2021); robustness with CISR (Wegmann et al., 2022).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of texts from different participants, separately within the unassisted human, post-edited, and original LLM-generated sets (p. 7, Figure 6). The PDF does not explicitly state whether all possible pairs are used or give their number. Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14) describes matching reference tasks where applicable.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are reported; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The PDF does not specify whether resampling preserves participant clusters or dependence between pairs sharing a writer.
diversity_detail.notes: H2a supports eligibility. Both human conditions use the same writers, not independent groups. Diversity directions are opposite to printed similarity-effect signs. The distribution is shown in Figure 6; no values have been estimated from the plot.

outcomes.name: Similarity to other participants’ post-edited writing versus own unassisted writing (H2c)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Diagnostic of shared post-edited style: the same post-edited texts are compared with other participants’ post-edited texts and with the author’s own unassisted control writing. This changes the reference source, not randomized treatment assignment (p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right). CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3). The PDF identifies the reference sources but does not specify whether the main test uses individual document-reference pairs or similarities aggregated within an output; the analysis unit remains null.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: other participants’ post-edited text)
contrasts.control_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: own unassisted text)
contrasts.reported: H2c, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 1.14, 95% CI [1.02, 1.26]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = 2.09, 95% CI [1.94, 2.24]. Post-edited text is more similar to other people’s post-edited text than to its author’s control text. The direction field indicates greater homogenization / lower stylistic distinctiveness; printed g is retained on the similarity scale.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.2 and Figure 5 right; p. 16, Table 3, H2c

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine stylistic similarity, contrasting an other-writer post-edited reference with an own-writer unassisted reference.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Post-edited treatment texts versus other participants’ post-edited texts and versus the same writer’s unassisted reference texts (p. 6, Figure 5 right). Appendix A.2 illustrates concatenated own-control references for H1a; it does not specify the full H2c reference aggregation or observation count (pp. 13-14). The main-test analysis unit is unconfirmed.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2); Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are reported; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. The PDF does not specify whether resampling preserves participant clusters or dependence between pairs sharing a writer.
diversity_detail.notes: This is a reference-source diagnostic, not an additional randomized AI-versus-no-AI estimate. Similarity and diversity directions are opposite.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to the author’s own unassisted writing (H1a)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Stylistic authenticity/self-similarity, not a creativity rating or within-person idea flexibility. Each treatment text before and after editing is compared with an embedding of that participant’s concatenated control texts (p. 13, Appendix A.2). CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3). Exploratory mixed models examine style importance (pp. 18-19, Table 4) and changes in linguistic acceptability (p. 21, Table 8); these are variants of the same output outcome. Appendix B.4 (pp. 17-18) additionally compares initial self-similarity across demographic subgroups and reports disagreement between embedding models. Appendix B.7.3 (p. 22) relates self-similarity change to the number, length, and total character volume of edits; these are associations, not additional assigned arms. The demographic comparisons in Appendix B.4 are comparisons of initial self-similarity across participant subgroups, not additional randomized AI-assistance contrasts.

contrasts.reported: H1a, LUAR-MUD: p = 0.0002, g = 0.55, 95% CI [0.38, 0.71]. CISR: p = 0.0002, g = 0.48, 95% CI [0.32, 0.64]. Table 4 exploratory post-edited (True): Estimate = 0.055, SE = 0.006, z = 9.167, p < .001, 95% CI [0.043, 0.066]; post-edited (True) x personal style importance (Non-max): Estimate = -0.017, SE = 0.013, z = -1.280, p = .201, 95% CI [-0.042, 0.009].
contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1a; p. 18, Table 4; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Individuality of stylistic alignment: own versus other participants’ unassisted reference text (H1a′)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Tests whether stylistic alignment after post-editing is specific to the author rather than generic human style. H1a-prime compares similarity to the author's own unassisted writing with similarity to other participants' unassisted writing, so it meets the codebook definition of diversity across different people's outputs (p. 3, section 3; p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5 left). The scored post-edited output was produced using an AI draft, so the question is across_people. Figure 5 left shows final similarity levels; section 6.1 also describes differences in stylistic shifts. CISR and the exploratory CoLA-adjusted reference-author model are variants of this endpoint (p. 16, Table 3; p. 21, Table 8). Table 8 is retained as a separate exploratory contrast because it models changes and codes own-reference versus other-reference, the reverse orientation of the displayed main comparison. The PDF does not settle whether the main H1a-prime g standardizes final levels or changes, or whether its main-test observations are individual pairs or scores aggregated within an output; unit remains null.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited text: similarity to others’ unassisted control writing
contrasts.control_arm: Same post-edited text: similarity to own unassisted control writing
contrasts.reported: H1a′: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.43]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.16]. The text states that editing moves writing more toward the author’s own style than other participants’ styles, and Figure 5 left shows lower similarity to others’ control writing. The printed sign is retained; confirm whether the reported test uses final levels or changes before effect extraction. Direction is coded on the inverse-similarity diversity convention: lower similarity to other writers gives treatment_higher. The printed effect and interval have not been re-signed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 5 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1a′

contrasts.reported: Exploratory mixed-effects model predicting change in stylistic similarity, Table 8: reference author (self) estimate = 0.027, SE = 0.004, z = 6.079, p < .001, 95% CI [0.018, 0.035]; CoLA difference estimate = -0.086, SE = 0.031, z = -2.777, p = .005, 95% CI [-0.147, -0.025]; CoLA difference x reference author (self) estimate = -0.116, SE = 0.040, z = -2.931, p = .003, 95% CI [-0.193, -0.038]. These are reference and moderator associations, not randomized aid contrasts. The positive self-reference coefficient denotes greater similarity change; its direction is treatment_lower on the inverse-similarity convention. This reference-author contrast does not estimate an effect of AI assistance.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine stylistic similarity to own versus other participants' unassisted writing; directions use the inverse-similarity convention for diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: The same post-edited texts are compared with their authors' own unassisted control writing and other participants' unassisted control writing (p. 6, Figure 5 left). Table 8 instead models change in similarity by same versus different reference author (p. 21). Appendix A.2 describes concatenated own-control references for H1a but does not establish the full H1a-prime reference aggregation, observation unit, or count (pp. 13-14).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Main comparisons use two-tailed permutation tests with 10,000 permutations (p. 13, Appendix A.2), with Hedges' g and 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples (p. 5, section 6). Raw p-values are reported; preregistered significance claims use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.05. Resampling units and handling of shared writers are not specified. The exploratory Table 8 mixed-effects model reports coefficients, SEs, z statistics, p-values, and intervals; its random-effects structure is not specified (p. 21, Appendix B.7.1).
diversity_detail.notes: These are reference-source diagnostics on AI-assisted outputs. Their direction fields use inverse similarity: lower similarity is coded higher and higher similarity is coded lower. Printed g values, coefficients, and intervals are unchanged. This convention does not turn the reference contrast into an AI-versus-no-AI effect; H2a remains the preferred randomized across_people contrast. The distinction between final similarity levels and changes remains open for the main H1a-prime effect.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity to LLM-generated writing / AI-likeness (H1b)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: LUAR-MUD cosine similarity to LLM-generated reference texts before versus after human post-editing (pp. 5-6, sections 5.2 and 6.1, Figure 3 left). CISR embeddings and Pangram AI-authorship likelihood are alternative measures of the same H1b claim and are grouped here as robustness variants (p. 16, Table 3). Appendix A.2 describes task-matched reference selection (pp. 13-14), but does not establish whether the main embedding test uses individual document-reference pairs or similarities aggregated within an output; its analysis unit remains null. Pangram separately uses an automated_score method on individual outputs, and its output-level unit and full reported statistics are retained within this grouped outcome. Table 5 (p. 18) is an exploratory moderation analysis by perceived style importance. AI-likeness does not itself measure creativity or diversity across people.

contrasts.locator: p. 5, section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3 left; p. 16, Table 3, H1b; p. 18, Table 5; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Post-edited text’s similarity to own unassisted style versus LLM style (H1c)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Compares the same post-edited text's similarity to its author's unassisted reference with its similarity to LLM-generated references. CISR and the exploratory reference-source/style-importance model are variants of this endpoint (p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right; p. 16, Table 3; pp. 18-19, Table 6 and Appendix B.5). This is a reference-source comparison, not AI-assisted versus unaided output quality. Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14) describes reference construction and task matching but does not establish whether the main H1c test uses individual document-reference pairs or similarities aggregated within an output; unit remains null. Table 6 calls the predictor same-participant (True), whereas its caption and Appendix B.5 describe human-versus-LLM reference source; the exact coding remains unresolved.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-edited LLM drafts (reference: own unassisted text)
contrasts.reported: H1c: LUAR-MUD p = 0.0002, g = -1.43, 95% CI [-1.55, -1.32]; CISR p = 0.0002, g = -2.30, 95% CI [-2.46, -2.15]. Post-edited text remains more similar to LLM-generated than own unassisted text. Exploratory mixed model, Table 6: same-participant (True) estimate = -0.125, SE = 0.005, z = -25.670, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.135, -0.116]; same-participant (True) x personal style importance (Non-max) estimate = -0.053, SE = 0.011, z = -4.977, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.073, -0.032]. Table 6 labels are transcribed as printed; its caption describes LLM-generated versus human-written reference sources. The exact reference coding of same-participant (True) is unresolved in the supplied document; no relabeling or signed reinterpretation of that coefficient has been made.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, section 6.1 and Figure 4 right; p. 16, Table 3, H1c; p. 18, Table 6; p. 19, Appendix B.5

outcomes.name: Linguistic acceptability of the final writing (CoLA score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory grammatical/linguistic acceptability scored by a Morris et al. (2020) model fine-tuned on expert human judgments from the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA); higher scores mean more acceptable text. This is a narrow language-quality measure, not an expert creativity rating (pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1 and Figure 12). Coded usefulness under the codebook inclusion of quality/appropriateness of a single output; this is specifically linguistic quality, not overall creativity or novelty.

contrasts.reported: The text states that post-edited writing is more linguistically acceptable than fully human-authored control text: p < .0001, g = -1.29, 95% CI [-1.57, -1.05]. The printed g sign is retained even though it is opposite to the treatment-minus-control direction used in this form; direction follows the prose and Figure 12.

The text states that post-edited writing is less linguistically acceptable than the original LLM-generated text: p < .0001, g = 0.59, 95% CI [0.45, 0.73]. The printed g sign is retained; direction follows the prose and Figure 12.

studies.label: Separate formative survey selecting personally meaningful writing scenarios

assignment.what_was_assigned: Only the presentation order of candidate writing scenarios was randomized. There was no assignment to AI assistance, no AI condition, and no scored writing task (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).
assignment.quote: These tasks were shown to participants in a randomized order.

arms.name: Formative scenario-selection survey
arms.description: All respondents selected scenarios where personal style matters; this was used to choose tasks for the main study (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

participants.exclusions: 102 people completed the formative survey; 88 passed its attention checks and were analyzed. The paper does not report a randomization-stage count (p. 23, Appendix C).
participants.who: Prolific participants who were not allowed to participate in the main study (p. 23, Appendix C).
participants.quote: 102 participants completed this formative survey of which 88 passed the attention checks.

ai_tool.how_used: No AI assistance was used in this formative scenario-selection survey (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).

task.description: From fifteen candidate writing scenarios plus two attention-check scenarios, participants selected eight options: six real scenarios and the two checks. No creative output was produced or scored. The authors used the preferences to select the eight main-study scenarios (pp. 22-23, Appendix C).
task.duration: Median completion time 3.53 minutes (p. 23, Appendix C).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper’s participants is stated. The main experiment and formative survey explicitly used non-overlapping samples.
sample_overlap.quote: Formative study participants were also recruited from Prolific, and were not allowed to also complete the main study.

company_involvement.description: Pangram provided API credits. All listed authors are affiliated with the University of Maryland; the acknowledgment also lists public research funding. Use of OpenAI models alone is not treated as evidence of OpenAI sponsorship.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria after final review: treatment/control block order is randomized (p. 4, section 4 and Figure 1), with four selected tasks randomly allocated to post-editing and two to unassisted writing (p. 24, Table 9); 81 unique people were analyzed and each contributed both conditions (p. 13, Appendix A.1; p. 24, Table 9); and H2a computes stylistic similarity between different participants' actual outputs (p. 5, section 5.2; p. 6, section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6). Participants produce treatment outputs by editing supplied generative-AI drafts (pp. 4-5, section 4 and Figure 2). The codebook includes writing tasks measured for across-writer similarity. S2 is a separate formative survey without AI assistance or scored creative output. Unconfirmed units for other outcomes and remaining reporting gaps do not affect these eligibility facts; participant-valid precision for pooling is not established.

one_line_finding: Among 81 analyzed writers, post-edited AI drafts were less stylistically diverse than unassisted writing (similarity Hedges’ g = 1.42, 95% CI [1.33, 1.51], p = .0002; sample: p. 13, Appendix A.1; result: p. 6, section 6.2 and p. 16, Table 3, H2a).
open_questions: The PDF reports recruitment, not a count explicitly at assignment, so main-study n_randomized remains null. Block-order sequence counts, the allocation algorithm, exclusion timing, and the breakdown by exclusion reason are not given (pp. 4, 13, 24). These details would require author confirmation; randomized blocks and 81 analyzed people are already documented.

Exact reference aggregation, pair enumeration, outcome observation counts, bootstrap/permutation resampling units, and mixed-model random effects are not fully specified. The main-test units for H2c (S1-O2), H1a-prime (S1-O4), H1b embeddings (S1-O5), and H1c (S1-O6) remain null; H2a/H2b are explicitly pair comparisons, H1a is output-level, and Pangram separately scores individual outputs. Participant-valid precision must not be assumed from the printed intervals (p. 5, section 6; pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2; p. 7, Figure 6; pp. 18-19, Tables 4-6 and Appendix B.5; p. 21, Table 8). Annotated posted data and analysis code would settle these analysis details.

Section 6.1 describes stylistic shifts, while Figure 5 left displays final similarity levels. The PDF does not fully establish which quantity Table 3's main H1a-prime effect standardizes (pp. 6, 16). The analysis script or labeled test inputs would settle this; H1a-prime is still an output-scored comparison across writers.

The printed CoLA g signs are opposite to a post-edited-minus-benchmark interpretation. The exact subtraction order is not stated; the prose establishes the directional ranking. Printed g and intervals are retained pending verification from analysis code or labeled contrast data (pp. 20-21, Figure 12 and Appendix B.7.1).

The unresolved reconciliation difference for S1-O6 persists: Table 6 names same-participant (True), but its caption and Appendix B.5 describe LLM-versus-human reference source. An explicit author-provided variable-coding definition would identify the exact coding; printed coefficients are retained verbatim (pp. 18-19).
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 using the current codebook and form specification, every c710 challenge file, the complete markdown conversion including references and Appendices A-D, and direct PDF text/table extraction. Eligibility facts, all retained main effect tuples, exploratory regression rows, and CoLA contrasts were checked against the saved PDF. No web source or unverified candidate-record claim was used. Only forms/c710.json was written. The saved document identifies arXiv v1; no later version was consulted. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical review provenance; the current fields and final.challenge_resolution record the final decisions. All three challenge problems are corrected: H1a-prime is diversity/across_people, its diversity details and inverse-similarity directions are explicit, and four unsupported main-test pair units are null. Correcting those unsupported values does not establish the underlying units; that source gap remains in open_questions and final.open_items. Main-study arm counts refer to the same 81 analyzed people and must not be added. The separate formative survey is not the eligible writing sample. Original LLM drafts are a reference stage rather than a third participant arm. Post-editing produces an AI-assisted output; no distinct delayed or post-removal test is reported. H1 and H2 are called the two main preregistered hypotheses, supporting paper_primary without asserting an independently verified preregistration's choice of a unique primary endpoint. H2a is the preferred across_people assistance contrast. Other reference-source and pre/post-editing comparisons do not add randomized aid contrasts. Printed statistics and signs are preserved; diversity direction fields use inverse similarity. The unknown resampling units prevent assuming participant-valid precision for pooling. Pangram remains grouped under H1b with its distinct automated, output-level method; CISR and exploratory mixed models remain variants of their corresponding outcomes. CoLA is a narrow linguistic-quality measure coded usefulness. Own-style and AI-style resemblance alone do not establish a creativity benefit. Self-reported authenticity, usability, workload, preferences, and formative scenario choices do not qualify as objective creativity/diversity outcomes. Authorship benchmarks and initial-generation consistency validate measurement/design; lexical counts and edit spans characterize editing. No eligible outcome is omitted because of the outcome cap. No country or separate code URL is stated. The final action counts refer to checker problems; the unchanged reconciliation counts refer to earlier A/B differences. All remaining open items affect extraction or interpretation, not eligibility.

a.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
a.description: The same analyzed participants supply content plans and edit an automatically generated LLM draft to express their personal style; four selected writing tasks per participant (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). Original unedited LLM drafts are retained as a reference stage, not a separately randomized arm.

a.name: Unassisted human control writing
a.description: The same analyzed participants plan and write without seeing any LLM-generated text; two selected writing tasks per participant (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9). This is the within-person control block, not a separate participant sample or a delayed follow-up.

b.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
b.description: Participants first planned content, then edited a supplied LLM-generated draft to express their personal style. Four tasks per participant; the same analyzed people also completed the control block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9).

b.name: Unassisted human writing
b.description: Participants planned content and wrote directly from those plans without seeing any LLM-generated text for those tasks. Two tasks per participant; these are the same people as in the treatment block (pp. 4-5, section 4; p. 24, Table 9).

b.name: LLM-generated drafts before post-editing
b.description: The original drafts supplied in the treatment tasks, retained as a pre-editing output benchmark. This is not a third randomized participant arm and contributes no additional people (p. 5, sections 4-6; pp. 6-7, Figures 3-6).

resolved.unedited_drafts: Reference-stage outputs within the treatment condition; no third participant arm.

differences.quote: In the treatment block, an LLM generates an initial draft (bottom, middle) which participants post-edit (bottom, right), and in the control block, participants write alone (top, middle and right).

resolved.detail: Full initial-draft generation from human-planned content, followed by human post-editing. The codebook ideas_supplied category concerns supplied ideas/examples.

differences.quote: In the treatment block, an LLM generates an initial draft (bottom, middle) which participants post-edit (bottom, right)
differences.locator: p. 4, Figure 2; pp. 4-5, sections 4 and 5.1; codebook section 6, AI role

differences.a: Participants choose six of eight personal writing scenarios and provide fictional planned details. Tasks include thank-you and apology letters, wedding/birthday speeches, catch-up and condolence letters, reassurance/encouragement messages, wedding vows, and eulogies/obituaries/tributes (p. 24, Table 9). separate_outcome.measure_detail: PANGRAM estimates the likelihood that an individual text is AI-authored (p. 5, section 5.2). grouped_under_H1b.measure_detail: LUAR-MUD cosine similarity to LLM-generated reference texts before versus after human post-editing (pp. 5-6, sections 5.2 and 6.1, Figure 3 left). CISR embeddings and Pangram AI-authorship likelihood are alternative measures of the same H1b claim and are grouped here as robustness variants (p. 16, Table 3). The primary embedding comparison involves text-reference pairs; Pangram instead scores individual outputs. Task-matched reference selection is described in Appendix A.2 (pp. 13-14); full aggregation details and observation counts are not given. Table 5 (p. 18) is an exploratory moderation analysis by perceived style importance. These scores do not by themselves measure creativity or diversity across people.

differences.a: Cosine similarity of each treatment text, before and after editing, to an embedding of that participant’s concatenated control texts (p. 13, Appendix A.2). This scores personal stylistic authenticity, not overall creativity or novelty. CISR is a robustness model (p. 16, Table 3); exploratory moderation by perceived style importance is in Table 4 (p. 18). Appendix B.7.3 (p. 22, Figure 13) reports associations of change in this same outcome with edit number/length, rather than additional creative outcomes.
differences.b: Stylistic authenticity/self-similarity, not a creativity rating or within-person idea flexibility. Each treatment text before and after editing is compared with an embedding of that participant’s concatenated control texts (p. 13, Appendix A.2). CISR is a robustness variant (p. 16, Table 3). Exploratory mixed models examine style importance (pp. 18-19, Table 4) and changes in linguistic acceptability (p. 21, Table 8); these are variants of the same output outcome. Appendix B.4 (pp. 17-18) additionally compares initial self-similarity across demographic subgroups and reports disagreement between embedding models. Appendix B.7.3 (p. 22) relates self-similarity change to the number, length, and total character volume of edits; these are associations, not additional assigned arms.
differences.resolved: Retain B’s reference to Appendix B.4 as an additional measurement diagnostic for stylistic self-similarity. It compares initial similarity across demographic subgroups and embedding models; it is not an extra randomized assistance outcome.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Exact assignment-stage count, block sequences/allocation algorithm, and exclusion timing/breakdown require authors' recruitment and allocation records. These gaps do not undo explicit randomization or the 81 analyzed people.

open_questions[1] and the unit challenge: Reference aggregation and main-test units for S1-O2/O4/O5/O6, pair enumeration and observation counts, resampling units, and mixed-model random effects require annotated data and analysis code. H2a already supplies a qualifying output-based diversity outcome.

open_questions[2]: Whether the main H1a-prime effect standardizes final similarity levels or changes requires the analysis script or labeled test inputs. This affects effect extraction, not outcome eligibility.
open_questions[3]: CoLA subtraction order requires analysis code or labeled contrast data. The prose establishes direction, printed numbers are retained, and eligibility rests on H2a.
